extracted.intended_audience: law students, legal scholars, and readers of English constitutional law (Blackstone)
extracted.subtask_description: A foundational exposition of the principal rights of Englishmen and the constitution and functioning of Parliament, describing substantive rights (life, liberty, property), procedural protections (habeas corpus, access to courts, petitioning), and rules for convening and composing Parliament. Aimed to guide understanding of English public law and constitutional limits on the crown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to personal security (life and limb)
rubrics_metrics.description: The immediate donation of the great Creator — life and limbs — cannot be legally disposed of or destroyed by any individual except by the direction of law; constitutions or laws that vest arbitrary power to kill or maim subjects are tyrannical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blackstone emphasizes that statute law very seldom, and the common law never, inflict punishments extending to life or limb except upon the highest necessity. Magna Carta: "Nullus liber homo ... aliquo modo destruatur, nisi per legale judicium parium suorum aut per legem terrae." Statutes 5 Edw. III. c.9 and 28 Edw. III. c.3 reinforce that no man shall be forejudged of life or limb or put to death without due process. Arbitrary execution, maiming, torturing, or oppression by colour of illegal authority is prohibited; laws directing destruction for light or trivial causes are also tyrannical (though lesser degree).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of torture and oppression under Magna Carta phrase "aliquo modo destruatur"
rubrics_metrics.description: The words "aliquo modo destruatur" (in Magna Carta) are interpreted to prohibit killing, maiming, torturing, and every oppression by colour of illegal authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Sir Edward Coke's interpretation (2 Inst. 48) that the phrase includes torture (to which English law is a stranger) and oppression; therefore such acts are inconsistent with the law of the land and Magna Carta protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Security from corporal insults (assaults, menaces, wounding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond life and major members, every person is entitled to security from corporal insults such as menaces, assaults, beating, and wounding, even when such acts do not amount to destruction of life or limb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These lesser personal wrongs are acknowledged as rights of the person; further branches and remedies are treated under personal wrongs in later commentaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to preservation of health
rubrics_metrics.description: A man's right includes preservation of health from practices that may prejudice or annoy it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed among personal rights; detailed treatments deferred to commentaries on personal wrongs and relevant torts/statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to security of reputation (protection from detraction and slander)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every man has a right to the security of his reputation or good name from the arts of detraction and slander, as necessary for enjoyment of other rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a recognized natural-rights-based protection; further discussion is referred to parts treating personal wrongs (defamation law).

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal liberty (freedom of locomotion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal liberty consists in the power of locomotion — changing situation or removing one's person to any place one pleases — without imprisonment or restraint except by due course of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law of England has not abridged this right without sufficient cause. Magna Carta: "no freeman shall be taken or imprisoned, but by the lawful judgment of his equals, or by the law of the land." Statutes and the Petition of Right (3 Car. I) and habeas corpus acts (e.g., 16 Car. I. c.10; 31 Car. II. c.2) protect against arbitrary detention; excessive bail is forbidden (1 W. & M. st.2 c.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Habeas corpus and requirements for lawful imprisonment
rubrics_metrics.description: To make imprisonment lawful it must be by process from courts of judicature or by warrant from a legal officer; warrants must be in writing, under hand and seal, and express the causes of commitment to permit habeas corpus inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no cause is expressed the gaoler is not bound to detain. Blackstone cites statutes and Coke (2 Inst. 52–53, 482) emphasizing written warrants and the right to call habeas corpus to have causes examined by King's Bench or Common Pleas. The habeas corpus act (31 Car. II c.2) provides methods preventing long detention except where law justifies it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to remain in the country; prohibition on forced exile
rubrics_metrics.description: Every Englishman may claim the right to abide in his own country and not be driven from it unless by sentence of the law; the king cannot send a subject out of the realm against his will except by express direction of statute or by the subject's choice (e.g., to avoid capital punishment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exile or transportation is unknown to the common law and only exists by modern acts of parliament; Magna Carta declares no freeman shall be banished except by judgment of peers or law of the land; habeas corpus statute forbids sending inhabitants beyond seas where common law protections are unavailable, punishable by praemunire and private actions with treble costs and damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of property (free use, enjoyment, and disposal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Property consists in the free use, enjoyment, and disposal of acquisitions, restrained only by laws of the land; private property's present forms are derived from society and are zealously protected by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magna Carta: no freeman shall be disseised or divested of his freehold except by judgment of peers or law of the land. Various ancient statutes prohibit seizure of lands or goods into the king's hands contrary to Magna Carta; dispossession without due process is redressable and void.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constraint on taking private property for public use (eminent domain with compensation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even for public benefit (e.g., making a road) the law will not permit taking private land without the owner's consent; when the legislature compels alienation it must give full indemnification and equivalent for the injury sustained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The public is to be treated as an individual bargaining with the owner; the legislature alone may compel transfer, and does so cautiously — property taken for public use requires reasonable price/compensation rather than arbitrary stripping.

rubrics_metrics.name: No taxation or aids without consent of the realm (parliamentary consent)
rubrics_metrics.description: No subject can be constrained to pay aids or taxes except those imposed by his own consent or that of his representatives in parliament; levying money for the crown by pretence of prerogative without grant of parliament is illegal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites statutes: 25 Edw. I. c.5–6, 34 Edw. I. st.4 c.1; 14 Edw. III. st.2 c.1; Petition of Right (3 Car. I) forbids compelled gifts/loans/benevolences/taxes without parliamentary consent; 1 W. & M. st.2 c.2 declares levying money for the crown without parliament illegal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Auxiliary subordinate rights protecting primary rights
rubrics_metrics.description: To secure enjoyment of personal security, liberty, and property the constitution establishes auxiliary subordinate rights: (1) powers and privileges of parliament, (2) limitation of the king's prerogative by known bounds, (3) right of access to courts, (4) right of petitioning, and (5) right to have arms suitable to condition and allowed by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are described as barriers that protect the three primary rights. Blackstone explains how each functions: parliament preserves legislative health; limits on prerogative guard executive power; courts provide redress; petitioning allows raising grievances; arms allow self-preservation when law insufficient. Statutory supports are cited (e.g., 1 W. & M. st.2 c.2 for arms and petitions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Access to courts and administration of justice (open courts; no sale/delay of justice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts of justice must be open to the subject; the law must be duly administered; every subject may take remedy by course of the law freely, fully, and speedily; the formal part of law (method of proceeding) cannot be altered except by parliament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magna Carta: "nulli vendemus, nulli negabimus, aut differemus rectum vel justitiam." Negative statutes (2 Edw. III. c.8; 11 Ric. II. c.10) prohibit commands under seals that disturb law; 1 W. & M. st.2 c.2 declares dispensing with laws by regal authority without parliament illegal. The king may erect new courts but they must follow established common law forms; statute 16 Car. I. c.10 on the starchamber dissolution forbids arbitrary proceedings to determine lands or goods outside ordinary courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to petition the king or either house for redress of grievances
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjects have a right to petition the king or either house of parliament for redress; petitioning is legal and prosecutions for petitioning are illegal, though some procedural restrictions exist to prevent riot or tumult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blackstone notes statutory limits (13 Car. II. st.1 c.5) restricting signatures on petitions (no more than 20 unless approved by local justices/grand jury, or by city authorities in London) and that only two persons present petitions at a time; 1 W. & M. st.2 c.2 protects the right to petition and declares commitments for petitioning illegal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to have and use arms for defence within legal limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjects have a right to have arms for their defence, suitable to their condition and degree, and such as are allowed by law; this is a public allowance of the natural right of resistance and self-preservation under due restrictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Declared by statute 1 W. & M. st.2 c.2; arms are allowed but subject to regulation to balance public order and individual self-defence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of legislative and executive powers as safeguard of liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the right of making and enforcing laws is vested in the same person or body, there can be no public liberty; the danger is that a magistrate might enact tyrannical laws and execute them tyrannically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blackstone argues that dividing the supreme power into distinct branches (legislative Parliament and executive king) prevents the executive from acquiring power that might subvert legislature and liberty. This principle underlies the British constitution's division into parliament (king, lords, commons) and the king as the executive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary composition and role (king, lords, commons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliament is the legislative branch consisting of king, lords, and commons; it is the proper repository of the supreme authority to make laws under the constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blackstone will consider manner/time of assembling, constituent parts, laws/customs as aggregate and for each house, methods of proceeding and making statutes, and adjournment/prorogation/dissolution. Historical origin and long-standing composition are noted (writs summoning knights, citizens, burgesses extant from 1266).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliament must be summoned by the king's writ (royal prerogative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliament is regularly to be summoned by the king's writ or letter issued out of chancery by advice of the privy council at least forty days before it begins to sit; no parliament can be convened by its own authority or by any authority except the king.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blackstone defends this royal prerogative: a single convoking authority avoids disputes over legitimacy if partial assemblies meet. He acknowledges extraordinary exceptions in cases of necessity (e.g., the Convention Parliament restoring Charles II, the convention in 1688 when throne deemed vacant) but treats them as exceptional and not precedent to diminish the crown's prerogative. Statute 16 Car. I. c.1 (now repealed) had attempted to allow peers to assemble if the king neglected for three years, but was repealed (16 Car. II. c.1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and timing of parliamentary writs and exceptional conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Writs should give forty days' notice and fix place/time. In emergencies (vacant throne, necessity), conventions or assemblies have met without regular royal writs, but such meetings are exceptional and often require subsequent validation by statute or royal assent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the convention-parliament that restored Charles II met before his return and was later declared valid by statute (12 Car. II c.1); 1688 convention under the Prince of Orange similarly arose from perceived vacancy. Blackstone emphasizes these are exceptions 'ex necessitate rei' and should not be treated as normal practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative forms and judicial forms cannot be altered except by Parliament
rubrics_metrics.description: Both the substantial/judicial decisions of law and the formal methods or course of proceeding are immutable except by Parliament; new courts must proceed according to established common law forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites statute 16 Car. I. c.10 (on starchamber dissolution) declaring that the king or privy council have no authority by English bill, petition, article, libel, or other arbitrary means to dispose of lands or goods — such matters must be tried in ordinary courts by course of law. This protects procedural regularity and prevents executive perversion of justice.
